Should Marijuana Users Come Out Of The Closet?

Analysis By Richard Cowan
October 11, 1998

The Human Rights Foundation, a Washington D.C. based gay rights organization, has declared that today is "National Coming Out Day" for gays and Lesbians.

Well, I have always said that there is a lot more smoke than sex in America’s closets these days.

This raises the question as to whether there should be a "Coming Out Day" for marijuana users.

Since I have experience with both closets, let me offer a little advice on safely opening doors.

First, it has to be acknowledged that everyone’s circumstances are different. It is a lot easier to come out in cities than in small towns. Where you work also makes a big difference, especially in the age of "drug" testing that is primarily aimed at marijuana users. And if you are a medical marijuana user, this is an added reason for caution. In short, as is with my fellow gays, I don’t buy the argument that "everyone" should come out. Some people really cannot.

That said, I am reminded of a quote that I saw – on a tee-shirt, of course, that said,
"You are only as sick as your secrets."

The expression "living a lie" conveys the corrosive effect of having to hide the truth.

As you might expect, I came out as a marijuana user a long time before I came out as being gay. This was the result of the 1972 National Review cover-article saying that Conservatives should support the legalization of marijuana. I didn’t actually announce that I was a marijuana smoker, but there was never any doubt about it.

The door on my other closet was badly damaged in 1986, when a month after my How the Narcs Created Crack cover –article, Buckley decided to run as a cover article a series of letters that I had written to him objecting to what I considered homophobic articles and editorials in NR. I was delighted, but the timing created a minor problem. The cover said that conservatives should support "gay rights."

He asked me if I wanted to use a pseudonym. I said yes, because I thought it would be unfair to both the marijuana reform and gay rights issues to have two cover articles a month apart that would have the effect of identifying the two really unrelated questions.

It was also an easy way out for me. Again, I did not proclaim in the article that I was gay. It was not relevant to the arguments. (I used the pseudonym, John Woolman, but my identity was never really a secret among the conservative leadership. Woolman was one of the first Quaker abolitionists. )

Unlike the 1972 article, the How the Narcs Created Crack piece drew very little opposition, even though this was in the middle of Nancy Reagan’s Just Say No campaign. On the other hand, the Woolman piece drew both touchingly grateful letters from some young gay conservatives and venomous responses from some on the religious right.

It wasn’t until I became National Director of NORML that I decided to formally come out as being gay. I thought that it was best to do this preemptively since some on the religious right are as rabidly prohibitionist as they are homophobic. I wasn’t going to give them the chance to "out" me. In Washington, only "secrets" about your sex life are news, as Clinton has learned the hard way, again.

Following a 1993 interview, the gay magazine, The Advocate, ran a banner across the top of its cover: "The King Of Pot Comes Out." Despite the silly headline, it was a well-written article that discussed the Woolman letters, and had several friendly quotes from my conservative friends.

The relevance of all this is that – if your circumstances allow it – how you come out makes a big difference. If you do it in the context of discussing the issues, people may assume that you are a marijuana user, even if you don’t say so. Of course, if you say that you smoked marijuana for years and never had any adverse consequences, this can be very effective. Most people will try to deal honestly with your arguments.  

In fact, some of the most effective anti-prohibitionist statements that I have heard have been made during the question periods at colleges after I have debated some narc who went through the usual reefer madness about how marijuana destroys the mind.

Invariably, some articulate young man – it is always a male – gets up and says, "I was my high school valedictorian and I have a 4.0 grade average and I have smoked everyday since I was in Junior high." Or something to that effect.

Since the narc didn’t have a 4.0 grade average – neither did I, but that was before I started smoking – they can only mumble a response.

One of the most effective things that an out of the closet marijuana-user can do is to confront a prohibitionist with the question, "How long do you think I should go to jail for? Do you think that this will be good for me or my family? Would that be a good use of prison resources?" Etc.

Don’t take it personally. Smile and laugh. It makes them look cruel and/or stupid, and it drives them nuts.

Also, remember that if you do come out, think about how you do it and of the impression that you will make on the marijuana reform movement. The movement is sometimes hurt by clowns who think more about "self-expression" than communication. This isn’t just about you. If it were, you wouldn’t have a chance.

Gays have the same problems with some of our more colorful brethren. However, the gay rights movement was not started by people who look like me. It was started by drag queens rioting when they got fed up with police harassment. People have the right to be themselves. The marijuana reform movement can learn a lot from the gay rights movement.

On the other hand, if you are not a marijuana user and you are just coming out as an anti-prohibitionist, then say that you are not a user. This will actually add credibility to your statements, even though logically it should not. One of the oddest things about all this is that there is a closet full of non-marijuana smoking anti-prohibitionists who are just afraid of being politically incorrect.

Former smokers are the most pathetic of this group. They have the knowledge, and credibility, and no risk at all. If someone who is successful says that they used to smoke and that it didn’t do them any harm, they can still go on to do anything, with the possible exception of running for President.

The fact is that a lot of people just stop enjoying marijuana – and alcohol. They should speak out, because they may need it or want it again when they get older. Most medical marijuana users don’t have conditions serious enough to warrant a prescription, any more than people need a prescription for aspirin, or a glass of wine in the evening. In short, you may need freedom later, so stand up for it now.

Things that you can do, even if you can’t come out.

  1. Join NORML. No, the DEA doesn’t have our membership list. If they did, what would they do with it? Not everyone who joins NORML smokes. That fact non-smokers join NORML makes smokers who don't join look all the more apathetic and/or cowardly. NORML only has around 5,000 members. If just one percent of the ten million or so regular marijuana users would join NORML, that would fundamentally change the nature of the battle.

  2. If you are a college student, join and/or organize a NORML chapter on your campus. On most major campuses there is absolutely no danger in being anti-prohibitionist. Have a no-smoking rule at your meetings. This reduces the danger and increases your credibility. Non-smokers will be more comfortable joining.  If the only reason that they join is to be able to smoke at meetings, you don't need them. People can smoke afterwards.

  3. If you have real security concerns, make an anonymous contribution to NORML in the form of a money order.

  4. Work on your communication skills, writing and using the Internet. Tell people that you meet on line about anti-prohibitionist web sites.

  5. Write letters to the editors of papers that publish reefer madness articles. To find out how to do that, see

www.mapinc.org
Some editors don’t seem to care about the truth, but they still don’t enjoy looking like fools. You can ask that they not use your name because anti-prohibitionists don’t have First Amendment rights in your area. That may make them think a little.

  • Write your politicians telling that they should inform themselves about how Dutch marijuana policies help fight drugs. They will send you a really stupid response, but don’t let it end there. Give them the facts. If they are conservatives, chide them for supporting a failed government policy ahead of "saving our children from drugs." Compare marijuana prohibition to communism. This is true, so it will confuse them.
    If they are liberals, attack the racist origins of marijuana prohibition, and the injustice of it. Compare marijuana prohibition to fascism. This is true, so it will confuse them.
    Most politicians vote for prohibitionist non-sense because they never hear any objection from our side. They also know that for every letter that they get there are hundreds of people who have the same opinion but don’t write.

  • Stop being defeatist when you are with other smokers. Defeatism becomes an excuse for doing nothing. What if gays had said to one another that we can never get equal rights? After all, we only make up about 2 or 3 percent of the population.

  • Consider stopping smoking so that you can fight for freedom. Which means more to you, freedom or getting high?
    Obviously, this does not apply to medical marijuana users. They cannot stop, just as gays cannot stop being gay. But if your situation is such that you cannot both smoke and speak-out, make a conscious choice. Speak out, but don’t whisper a curse against the darkness.

The real reason that marijuana is illegal is not because of anything that the narcs do.

Marijuana is illegal because of what marijuana users do not do. We do not stand up for our freedom.

Finally, consider this quote from Peter McWilliams’ new site

http://www.lungrendoyourduty.com/
